name: DeepSeek V4.1 sibling fused ops catalogue (vLLM hand-fused stack: nvidia/ and common/)
scope: Static read of every hand-fused op in vLLM's DeepSeek V4.1 NVIDIA model package: nvidia/ops/{mega_mhc,mhc,fused_wo_a,o_proj,engram_peer}.py, nvidia/ops/cute_dsl/{all_reduce_mhc,primitives}.py (CuTe DSL, the DSL MegaBake bodies are written in), nvidia/{flashinfer_sparse,flashmla,flash_mla_mega_attn,dspark,decoder_replay_cudagraph,model,model_state}.py, the shared decoder_replay_layers.py, and common/{engram.py, rope.py, ops/*} (fused_compress_quant_cache, query_quant, indexer_k_store, fused_layout, cache_utils), plus the TileLang mHC kernels they dispatch to (vllm/model_executor/kernels/mhc/tilelang.py). For each op: what it fuses, data formats, why, measured numbers in comments, and a classification: (a) generic and compiler-expressible, (b) megakernel-favoured or megakernel-exclusive, (c) inherently model-specific. Question answered for MegaBake: which of these hand fusions are patterns a generic megakernel compiler should learn (and which CuTe DSL idioms can be copied into MegaBake bodies), which are only worth it because vLLM runs hundreds of kernels, and how vLLM runs decode/spec decode around them. Key correction to the brief: decoder_replay_cudagraph.py is NOT the decode path. It is prefill-side 'SWA bounded replay' (row trimming for layers past the last KV-source layer). Decode in this stack is FULL CUDA graphs plus multi-stream overlap inside the graph, and spec decode is DSpark (block-parallel draft plus a sequential Markov head). No GPU jobs were run. Every number below is quoted from source comments and was measured on GB200/GB300 (SM100), not on the H200 MIG slice.

core_ideas.idea: Mega mHC: shifted mHC post + next mHC pre + RMSNorm in one DeepGEMM kernel (mega_mhc.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: One SM100 DeepGEMM launch takes the sublayer output x [T,H] BF16 and the hc=4 residual streams [T,4,H] BF16. (1) It applies the mHC post-mix new_res[t] = post[t]*x + sum_s comb[s,t]*res[s] and writes new_residual. (2) From registers, it runs the next block's pre: a TF32 'prenorm' GEMM of the 4H-wide stream against fn [24, 4H] FP32 (mix_size = hc*(hc+2)) plus a sum of squares for RMS. (3) Scale/base/sigmoid-style mix generation and num_sinkhorn_iters Sinkhorn normalization of the 4x4 comb matrix per token. (4) Collapse of the streams with the carried (shifted) pre-mix, then RMSNorm with the layer norm weight to a BF16 layer input y_bf16. It also emits new_prev_mix / new_post_mix / new_comb_res_mix for the next boundary. Dispatch order in mhc.py: overlap path (FULL graph, <= 16 tokens) > Mega mHC > TileLang fused post+pre fallback.
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16 activations and residual streams; FP32 mix coefficients, fn and bases; TF32 MMA for the 24-wide projection; BF16 normalized output.
core_ideas.why: The mHC boundary is a residual add, a skinny GEMM, a tiny per-token 4x4 iterative normalization and an RMSNorm. Unfused, that is 4-6 launches and 2-3 passes over a 4H-wide stream per sublayer, twice per layer. Fusing reads the 4H stream once.
core_ideas.classification: (c) for the mHC math. The fusion SHAPE is (a): an epilogue that updates the residual, feeding a reduction GEMM prologue, then a norm. This is the same structure as 'residual add + RMSNorm + next GEMM prologue' in any transformer, and a compiler with prologue/epilogue fusion and register-resident producer->consumer can express it.

core_ideas.idea: Delayed/shifted mHC coefficients computed off the critical path on a side stream (mhc.py overlap path)
core_ideas.how_it_works: Because the pre-mix is 'delayed' (each sublayer collapses with the PREVIOUS sublayer's pre-mix), the coefficient GEMM + Sinkhorn for the next boundary does not block the current layer input. mhc_pre_delayed_overlap splits the TileLang/DeepGEMM epilogue into split_mode='input' (collapse + RMSNorm, on the caller stream) and split_mode='stats' (tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm + coefficient generation, on mhc_stream). For n <= 8 the input half is issued before forking so the critical path starts first. The decoder layer joins the stream (wait_stream) after attention and after the FFN. Enabled only when capturing FULL CUDA graphs with 0 < tokens <= 16. PIECEWISE graphs and eager mode fall back to Mega mHC.
core_ideas.data_formats: Same as above; split-K partial mix [splits, T, 24] FP32 and sqr [splits, T] FP32 scratch.
core_ideas.why: At decode the coefficient GEMM is tiny and latency-bound. Running it concurrently with attention/MoE hides it.
core_ideas.measured_numbers_in_source: mhc.py:36: 'GB200 TP4/FlashInfer improves through 16 tokens; larger screens tie or regress.' No absolute numbers.
core_ideas.classification: (b) megakernel-favoured. In a megakernel this is a dependency-graph fact (the stats task depends only on the residual, and its consumer is one sublayer later), so idle workers can run it with an event counter. Multi-kernel needs stream fork/join inside a FULL graph and only pays at <= 16 tokens. Expressible by a compiler that schedules a task DAG (generic), but only cheap with fine-grained events.

core_ideas.idea: Lamport all-reduce fused with mHC post, collapse and RMSNorm (CuTe DSL all_reduce_mhc.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: Two PDL-chained kernels. Publish kernel: each rank reads its BF16 partial, replaces -0.0 with +0.0 (sanitize), and writes it with multimem.st (NVLink multicast) into slot [generation][rank][token] of a symmetric-memory mailbox on every peer. Consumer kernel (grid = tokens x cluster of 5 CTAs x 128 threads): BEFORE griddepcontrol_wait it preloads gamma, the 4 residual streams and the post/pre/comb mixes into registers. It then spins with ld.volatile.v4 on each rank's slot until no BF16 -0.0 sentinel remains (the data itself is the ready flag; there is no separate flag or barrier). It sums the ranks in FP32, rounds to BF16 (to match the unfused collective), applies the mHC post-mix (4x4 comb + post*x) and stores the residual streams, collapses with the pre-mix, and stores prenorm in registers. It advances the generation counter (3 generations, so the next call's writes never alias a slot still being read), calls launch_dependents, and re-arms its slots with the sentinel. Finally it computes the row's sum of squares: warp shuffles, then the SMEM block sum, then a cluster-wide sum via mapa + st.shared::cluster into each peer's SMEM slot, then cluster_arrive/wait, then rsqrt and normalize to the BF16 layer input. The finalize variant additionally folds the MoE top-k combine into the publish: it gathers the permuted GEMM2 rows by expanded_idx_to_permuted_idx (-1 means not on this rank), weights them by FP32 routing weights (prefetching all top_k rows first), and adds the shared-expert output.
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16 contributions in a [3, tp, capacity=16, hidden] BF16 symmetric mailbox, BF16 -0.0 (0x8000) sentinel, FP32 accumulation, FP32 mixes, BF16 outputs; MoE: BF16 permuted GEMM2 rows, FP32 routing weights, int32 permutation.
core_ideas.why: At <= 16 tokens a TP all-reduce is pure latency. One-shot Lamport removes the flag round trip, and folding post/collapse/norm (and the MoE finalize) into the consumer removes 2-4 kernels and several hidden-size passes per boundary.
core_ideas.measured_numbers_in_source: Presets copied from FlashInfer 'LL_ALL_REDUCE_GB300_TP{4,8}_H5120' (all_reduce_mhc.py:882-885). No timings in the file. The only gate number is MHC_OVERLAP_MAX_TOKENS = 16 (GB200 TP4).
core_ideas.classification: Communication part: (a)/(b). The 'all-reduce + residual + RMSNorm' epilogue fusion is generic (vLLM already has a compiler pass for AllReduce+RMSNorm). Data-as-flag Lamport sync is a generic runtime primitive that is only safe when consumer and producer are co-resident (megakernel or PDL). The mHC and MoE-finalize parts are (c). The cluster-DSMEM row reduction is (a) and directly reusable.

core_ideas.idea: Cluster-wide row reduction through DSMEM instead of a grid barrier (inside all_reduce_mhc consumer)
core_ideas.how_it_works: A token row of 5120 BF16 = 640 16-byte fragments is split over a cluster of 5 CTAs x 128 threads, one fragment per thread, one trip. Each CTA reduces its sum of squares (shuffle_sync_bfly over the warp, then a warp-0 reduction of SMEM warp sums). Thread i < cluster_size then writes the CTA sum into CTA i's cluster_sums[cluster_rank] with mapa.shared::cluster + st.shared::cluster.f32, and the cluster syncs with cluster_arrive/cluster_wait. Every CTA then has the full row sum locally, without a global-memory round trip or a grid barrier.
core_ideas.data_formats: FP32 partial sums in SMEM; BF16 data in registers.
core_ideas.why: It spreads a single-token norm over more SMs (more load bandwidth and more threads) without the cost of a cross-CTA barrier.
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic, hardware-feature dependent (SM90+ clusters). A compiler can emit it whenever a reduction axis is split across <= 8 (portable) or <= 16 (non-portable) CTAs.

core_ideas.idea: Fused WO-A: inverse RoPE + MXFP8 quant prologue, cluster split-K tcgen05 block-scaled GEMM, MXFP8 requant epilogue (CuTe DSL fused_wo_a.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: Grid = n_tiles * heads_per_group CTAs x token_tiles, with cluster = heads_per_group (<= 8). Each CTA owns one head (K = 512) of one group for one 128-wide N tile. Warp 0 first issues TMA for all 4 K stages of the FP8 weight tile and its raw per-32 scales. This happens BEFORE griddepcontrol_wait because weights do not depend on the predecessor, so weight loads overlap the previous kernel's tail. After the wait it allocates TMEM (allocating earlier could deadlock against a PDL predecessor holding TMEM). All threads hoist every token's BF16 x loads and the cos/sin loads, then apply inverse RoPE on the last 64 dims with inline-PTX mul.rn + fma.rn so rounding matches the unfused kernel. They take amax over 8-lane groups (32 elements = one MX block), compute the UE8M0 exponent with cvt.rp.satfinite.ue8m0x2 and 2^-e via bit arithmetic, and quantize to E4M3 into 128B-swizzled SMEM plus scale bytes. Each stage's mbarrier waits on the TMA bytes plus threads/4 quantizer arrivals. The MMA warp transposes the weight scales into UTCCP order in SMEM (TMA cannot scatter at 4-byte granularity), fences, issues tcgen05.cp for both scale tiles into TMEM, and issues 4 tcgen05.mma_mxfp8 (K = 32 each) per stage, with M = 128 weight rows and N = padded token count (swapAB orientation). Epilogue: tcgen05.ld the FP32 accumulator, then st.async each token's partial into the owning peer CTA's SMEM (token % heads_per_group) with mbarrier transaction counting. The owner sums the peers' partials, rounds to BF16, requantizes to MXFP8 with warp_redux max, and writes FP8 output plus scale bytes in FlashInfer's F8_128x4 swizzled layout. It also zeros the scale padding itself ('no second memset kernel'). launch_dependents fires at the last MMA stage. Host: compile keys per (tokens_per_tile, token_tiles, full_tiles, groups, heads_per_group, rank), at most 46 keys for T = 1..96, pre-warmed via WarmupIntRange tracing.
core_ideas.data_formats: In: attention output BF16 [T, H, 512] (448 NoPE + 64 RoPE), int64 positions, FP32 cos||sin cache; weight FP8 E4M3 [groups*rank, heads_per_group*512] with int32-packed UE8M0 per-32 scales (DeepGEMM MN-major). Out: FP8 E4M3 [T, groups*rank] plus UE8M0 bytes in F8_128x4 layout consumed directly by FlashInfer's CuTe DSL MXFP8 wo_b GEMM.
core_ideas.why: For small decode batches the grouped O-projection is weight-bandwidth bound and spread over few tiles. Splitting K across a cluster multiplies CTAs (n_tiles x heads_per_group). Fusing inverse RoPE and both quantizations removes 2-3 launches and two HBM round trips of the activation. Emitting wo_b's native scale layout removes a re-layout kernel.
core_ideas.measured_numbers_in_source: Only the heuristic in o_proj.py:20-24: 'Additional token tiles only pay off for smaller grids' gives 96 tokens if ctas_per_tile <= 128, else 32. No timings.
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic: a prologue (pointwise + quant into the A/B operand), split-K over a cluster with DSMEM reduction, and an epilogue quant into the consumer's layout. A compiler with prologue/epilogue templates can express all three. Inverse RoPE on a 448/64 split head is (c) but is just a pointwise prologue. Issuing weight TMA before the dependency wait is the multi-kernel shadow of a megakernel's cross-phase weight prefetch (b).

core_ideas.idea: CuTe DSL primitive kit (primitives.py): raw PTX building blocks and graph-safe launch helpers
core_ideas.how_it_works: Inline-asm wrappers via llvm.inline_asm + dsl_user_op: ld.global.v4/v2.u32 (optionally ld.volatile for polling), ld.global.b16 + cvt.f32.bf16, st.global.v4.u32, the Lamport sentinel store, BF16 negative-zero sanitize/detect helpers, mapa.shared::cluster + st.shared::cluster.f32, cvt.rn.bf16.f32, shfl.sync.idx marked side-effecting so later divergent consumers keep full-warp execution, and multimem.st.relaxed.sys.global.{bf16x2, v2, v4}. Host helpers: _GraphSafeDLPack calls tensor.__dlpack__(stream=-1) so from_dlpack does not insert a producer-stream sync during CUDA graph capture. to_cute_dynamic marks the leading dim dynamic with a divisibility hint. make_fake_dynamic_compact_tensor uses sym_int32 for compile-once-per-shape-class. cute.compile is called once at init with fake tensors.
core_ideas.data_formats: u32x4 = 8 BF16, u32x2 = 4 BF16; BF16 sentinel 0x8000.
core_ideas.why: CuTe DSL lacked (at the time) first-class ops for volatile vector loads, cluster remote stores and multicast stores. Raw PTX keeps exact instruction control.
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic infrastructure, directly reusable in MegaBake bodies (ld.volatile polling, DSMEM remote store, vectorized raw ld/st, graph-safe dlpack, dynamic-dim fake tensors). Only multimem.* is multi-GPU-specific.

core_ideas.idea: MoE top-k finalize deferred into the next boundary (model.py defer_finalize + finalize publish)
core_ideas.how_it_works: When the experts are TRTLLM MXFP4 modular and routed_scaling_factor == 1, the MoE stops after GEMM2 and returns UnfinalizedMoEOutput (permuted rows, FP32 weights, permutation, shared-expert output). The next layer's first mHC boundary runs AllReduceMHC.finalize, whose publish kernel does the weighted top-k gather-sum + shared-expert add while it multicasts. This is skipped before Engram layers and for the last layer (no successor boundary).
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16 GEMM2 rows in permuted order, FP32 routing weights, int32 index map.
core_ideas.why: It removes the finalize kernel and one full write + read of [T, hidden] per layer.
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic 'consumer-side reduction of a producer's unreduced output' (sink a reduction into the consumer's prologue). The MoE details are (c).

core_ideas.idea: Two-cache sparse attention in one call + per-step planner metadata shared across same-type layers (flashmla.py, flashinfer_sparse.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: FlashMLA decode: one flash_mla_with_kvcache call attends over SWA indices into the sliding-window FP8 cache plus 'extra' compressed-cache top-k indices produced by the indexer layer, with attn_sink. Queries in the same sequence are treated as separate queries over generated indices. Tile-scheduler metadata (tile_sched_swaonly / c1a / c2a) is computed by the in-kernel planner on the first layer of each compress_ratio type in a step. It is allocated with the graph-aware allocator so captured graphs reuse addresses, and later same-type layers skip the planner. h_q is zero-padded to 64 or 128 because the FP8 decode kernel only supports those. FlashInfer TRTLLM-gen path: keeps the decode/prefill split because 'the launcher is tuned for uniform-q batches'. Metadata buffers are preallocated so graphs keep addresses. For DSpark's non-causal draft block it clamps topk lens to at least window and exposes the full block per query.
core_ideas.data_formats: FP8 KV cache records (SWA and compressed; NVFP4 288-byte compressed record on the mega-attn path), BF16 or FP8 Q, int32 indices.
core_ideas.why: Amortize planning across ~60 layers per step, and keep everything CUDA-graph capturable with fixed addresses.
core_ideas.classification: Attention kernels themselves: library (c, DSA-specific sparse MLA). 'Plan once per step, reuse across layers of the same type' is (a) generic and is the runtime analogue of a megakernel's static tile map.

core_ideas.idea: Mega attention: Q RoPE + sparse attention + inverse RoPE + FP8 cast in one kernel, with load-time weight permutations (flash_mla_mega_attn.py, common/ops/fused_layout.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: The kernel RoPEs Q itself, so the KV-insert path only zero-pads Q heads. It inverse-RoPEs the output and casts it to FP8 straight into wo_a's input buffer. wq_b rows and wo_a columns are permuted once at load (Q in 16-element head-dim chunks interleaved across heads; O in 32-element chunks interleaved across the 8 heads of a wo_a group), so the producing and consuming GEMMs read and write the kernel's layouts with no per-step shuffle.
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16 Q in, FP8 output with scales (QuantizedActivation), NVFP4 compressed KV record.
core_ideas.why: Remove the RoPE, inverse-RoPE and quant kernels around attention, and avoid any transpose between attention and its neighbouring GEMMs.
core_ideas.measured_numbers_in_source: GB300, CUDA graphs on, mega vs split-KV us per step (64-head model, topk_swa=128, topk_extra=512): TP1 s_q=1: 29/29, 32: 31/31, 128: 31/40, 256: 53/72, 512: 96/140 (up to 1.45x). TP2-TP8 within a few percent, with a ~2 us penalty at small s_q because cost scales with padded heads (64). 'Measure under CUDA graphs: in eager mode launch overhead swamps both paths and overstates the fused one several-fold.'
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic. Layout propagation (choosing a GEMM's output layout to match its consumer, applied as a compile-time weight permutation) and pointwise prologue/epilogue fusion into attention are standard compiler transforms. The specific chunk sizes are (c).

core_ideas.idea: Horizontal fusion and multi-stream concurrency of independent input projections (model.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: Stacked weights: wq_a|wkv become fused_wqa_wkv, and compressor wkv|wgate become fused_wkv_wgate (one GEMM per shared input). Three aux streams run the remaining independent input GEMMs (compressor kv_score, indexer weights_proj) concurrently with fused_wqa_wkv. On SM90 with custom all-reduce, large batches shard fused_wqa_wkv by token and all-gather. GEMM-RS (CuTe DSL fused wo_b GEMM + reduce-scatter over NVLink multicast) runs under sequence parallel. Engram host-table lookups run on a background stream with grid = num_SMs // 2 'to leave SMs for the main stream'.
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16/FP8/MXFP8 GEMM inputs as per layer quant config.
core_ideas.why: Decode-time small GEMMs underfill the GPU. Concurrency or horizontal stacking fills SMs.
core_ideas.measured_numbers_in_source: Engram thresholds 'Measured on GB200': sort from 36864 rows, inline from 4096 tokens (engram.py:93-99).
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic (horizontal fusion of same-input GEMMs; concurrent independent tasks). SM partitioning between a background task and the main stream is (b): a megakernel controls it exactly via worker assignment, while streams only hint at it.

core_ideas.idea: Other common/ fused ops: Q/KV RMSNorm + MXFP8 quant, compressor pool + RMSNorm + state save, RoPE + quant + paged insert, indexer k_norm + RoPE + MXFP4/FP8 quant + store
core_ideas.how_it_works: Triton kernels, one program per row or token. fused_q_kv_rmsnorm_quant normalizes both Q and KV rows and writes Q as MXFP8 with FlashInfer's swizzled F8_128x4 scale layout [row/128, group/4, row%32, row%128/32, group%4]. fused_save_compress_norm pools each closed group of compress_ratio tokens into a normalized BF16 latent and saves FP32 [kv, score] ring rows. rope_quant_insert applies GPT-J RoPE and quantizes into the paged compressed cache only at group boundaries. indexer_k_norm_rope_store does k_norm, RoPE at the group's first position, MXFP4/FP8 quant and the paged store.
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16 in; MXFP8 / MXFP4 / FP8 UE8M0 out; FP32 state rings; paged caches.
core_ideas.why: Each removes 2-4 elementwise launches and keeps quant scale layouts in the consumer's native format.
core_ideas.classification: (a) generic (norm + pointwise + quant + scatter chains are textbook Inductor fusions). The compression schedule is (c).

core_ideas.idea: SWA bounded replay: run layers past the last KV-source layer only on each request's last `window` rows (decoder_replay_layers.py + decoder_replay_cudagraph.py + model_state.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: In prefill, the last KV-source layer writes KV for all rows (write_kv runs only its mHC pre + attention KV path). Later layers only own sliding-window KV and only the last token's logits are needed, so they run on a gathered sub-batch: each request's last `window` rows, with its own attention metadata and forward context, like a microbatch. Outputs are scattered back into zero-filled full-size tensors (trimmed rows are never read). Under PIECEWISE graphs, graphs at or above trim_threshold break out (eager_break_during_capture) to the replay batch. That batch can run in its own breakable PIECEWISE CUDA graph keyed by padded replay size; sizes step by `window`, then by 1/8 of the power-of-two interval (e.g. 256 in [2048, 4096)). Inputs are copied into static buffers with index_select. FULL graphs and small PIECEWISE graphs keep the whole batch.
core_ideas.data_formats: Same activations; int64 row indices; persistent int32 replay_start buffers.
core_ideas.why: This is dead-row elimination in prefill. For long prompts with a 128-token window, the tail layers do O(window) rather than O(prompt) work.
core_ideas.classification: (c) as implemented (depends on per-layer KV ownership). The underlying principle is (a): liveness-based row trimming. Rows whose values reach no live output (logits for the last token, KV caches still needed) can be dropped after the last layer that needs them. For dense full-attention models only the final norm and lm_head can be trimmed (HF logits_to_keep). For hybrid sliding-window models such as Gemma 3, layers after the last global layer could be trimmed.

core_ideas.idea: DSpark speculative decoding: block-parallel draft with context-KV precompute, non-causal block attention through sparse indices, sequential Markov head, confidence head (dspark.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: The draft is 3 DSV4.1 decoder layers (checkpoint mtp.* weights) that share the target's embedding and lm_head. combine_hidden_states = main_norm(main_proj(concat of target aux hidden states from dspark_target_layer_ids)). precompute_and_store_context_kv runs each draft layer's fused_wqa_wkv (keeping only the KV part), kv_norm and the fused RoPE/quant/insert to write context KV from the projected target hidden. The draft block is then decoded in ONE parallel pass. Non-causal attention is implemented by putting future query positions into the sparse top-k index set (flashinfer_sparse.py non-causal lens). After the layers: mhc_post, then hc_collapse with the last FFN pre-mix. A low-rank Markov head (V x r, r x V, replicated so no all-reduce per position) adds a transition bias to the candidate logits left to right. It is applied only to gathered candidate rows via an NVFP4 gathered-bias Triton kernel. A confidence head (linear over [hidden, markov_embed]) estimates acceptance per position; model_state notes 'Adaptive verification may lengthen the decodes on the device'. Target aux hidden states are read back from the fused mHC pre kernel ('every layer's post runs inside the next layer's fused pre') rather than recomputed.
core_ideas.data_formats: BF16 hidden, FP8 KV, NVFP4 W4A16 Markov projection weights, FP32 confidence projection.
core_ideas.why: Decode is weight-bandwidth bound. Verifying k+1 tokens costs nearly the same as 1, so drafting a block in one pass plus a cheap sequential head gives multi-token steps.
core_ideas.classification: (c) algorithm- and model-specific. Megakernel relevance: target verification is just decode with T = k+1 rows (fits MegaBake's <= 64-row swapAB path), and a draft-verify loop is a strong megakernel-exclusive candidate (see opportunities).

core_ideas.idea: Decode execution model: FULL CUDA graphs with in-graph multi-stream overlap and PDL chaining (model.py, model_state.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: Decode steps replay FULL CUDA graphs. Inside them, mHC coefficient work forks onto mhc_stream and joins with wait_stream. Attention input GEMMs use 3 aux streams. Hand kernels chain with programmatic dependent launch (griddepcontrol_wait / launch_dependents in fused_wo_a and all_reduce_mhc), and each does dependency-free work (weight TMA, residual/gamma/mix preloads) before its wait. Every buffer a graph reads is persistent (lookback ids, replay buffers, FlashInfer metadata). DP ranks agree on graph size. Shapes: JIT warmup registry pre-compiles every kernel variant for every token count the dispatcher can produce.
core_ideas.why: It approximates a megakernel's absence of launch gaps (graphs) and its cross-op overlap (PDL prologues, streams) while keeping per-op specialized kernels.
core_ideas.measured_numbers_in_source: mhc.py:36 (overlap helps only through 16 tokens on GB200 TP4).
core_ideas.classification: (b) This is exactly what a megakernel subsumes. PDL only overlaps a kernel with its immediate predecessor's tail, and streams give uncontrolled SM sharing. A persistent kernel with event counters gets arbitrary-depth overlap with explicit SM assignment.

core_ideas.idea: Engram peer exchange over symmetric memory (engram_peer.py)
core_ideas.how_it_works: Each rank in the node-local Engram DP group copies its token hashes into a symmetric int32 buffer and barriers. A Triton kernel reads every peer's hashes through a pointer table and looks up this rank's shard of hash heads (vocab range per layer from a metadata table). It writes packed rows of FP8 values + UE8M0 scale bytes (dim + dim/32 bytes) into a symmetric output buffer, and barriers again. Peers read rows through row_ptrs.
core_ideas.data_formats: int32 hash ids; uint8 FP8 rows with per-32 UE8M0 scales.
core_ideas.why: It shards a huge n-gram embedding table across DP ranks without NCCL all-to-all for small slots.
core_ideas.classification: (c) model- and multi-GPU-specific. Not applicable to MegaBake's single-GPU scope.

megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.opportunity: Float off-critical-path tasks (vLLM's delayed mHC coefficient GEMM, Engram lookups) onto idle workers, with event-counter dependencies
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.why_multi_kernel_cannot_match: vLLM forks a side stream inside a FULL CUDA graph. The side-stream kernels compete for SMs with whatever the main stream runs, with no control over placement, and each fork/join adds graph edges and a launch. vLLM measured a gain only up to 16 tokens on GB200 TP4 (mhc.py:36); above that the overhead ties or regresses. Engram hard-codes grid = num_SMs // 2 to 'leave SMs for the main stream' (engram.py:1140-1142), a static guess. A persistent kernel can assign exactly the workers that would otherwise spin at a barrier, and can start the task the moment its producer counter is reached.
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.nearest_multi_kernel_substitute: Multi-stream inside CUDA graphs plus PDL. It hides small work at <= 16 tokens but cannot guarantee SM partitioning or zero fork/join cost.

megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.opportunity: Arbitrary-depth weight prefetch (TMA into SMEM or L2) for the next GEMM while waiting on its activation dependency
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.why_multi_kernel_cannot_match: fused_wo_a issues weight TMA before griddepcontrol_wait (fused_wo_a.py:213-229). This only works one kernel deep, only once the dependent grid has actually been launched and its CTAs are resident next to the predecessor's, and it needs care (TMEM allocation after the wait to avoid deadlock, fused_wo_a.py:230-235). In a persistent kernel every worker is resident and knows its next phases statically (table), so it can prefetch weights of phase i+1 or i+2 during any barrier wait.
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.nearest_multi_kernel_substitute: PDL with dependency-free prologue (overlaps only the immediate predecessor's tail), or cudaGraph L2 persistence/access-policy windows.

megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.opportunity: Data-as-flag (Lamport sentinel) producer/consumer synchronization instead of counter barriers
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.why_multi_kernel_cannot_match: Spinning on data is only safe if the producer is guaranteed to make progress while consumers spin. Across kernels this needs PDL early launch, and a consumer grid occupying SMs can starve the producer. vLLM confines it to tiny grids (tokens x 5 CTAs). In a cooperative persistent kernel all workers are co-resident by construction, so a consumer tile can poll its exact input fragments (pre-filled with a sentinel such as -0.0 or a NaN payload, re-armed by the consumer). There is no separate flag write or fence round trip.
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.nearest_multi_kernel_substitute: Stream ordering or PDL griddepcontrol.wait, which waits for the whole predecessor grid.

megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.opportunity: Draft-verify speculative decoding loop inside one launch
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.why_multi_kernel_cannot_match: DSpark's sequential Markov head and acceptance are tiny per-position ops with data-dependent control (adaptive verification length). vLLM must run them as separate graph replays or host-side decisions. A megakernel can run target verification (T = k+1 rows, weight-bandwidth bound, so nearly free versus T = 1) and the draft forward plus acceptance in one launch, branching on device. That removes per-step host round trips, which are MegaBake's own main advantage today.
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.nearest_multi_kernel_substitute: CUDA graphs per fixed draft length plus device-side conditional graph nodes (CUDA 12.4+), or host-side acceptance between replays.

megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.opportunity: Cross-'kernel' epilogue/prologue fusion without hand-writing a fused kernel (e.g. deferred MoE finalize, all-reduce + post + norm)
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.why_multi_kernel_cannot_match: Strictly speaking this is a compiler property, not a runtime one: vLLM achieves it by hand-writing a new fused kernel per pair. In a megakernel compiler the 'kernel boundary' is just a barrier between phase bodies, so a producer's unreduced output can be consumed directly from L2 by the next body's prologue without a new template. Not truly exclusive; flagged so it is not over-claimed.
megakernel_exclusive_opportunities.nearest_multi_kernel_substitute: Hand-fused kernels (vLLM) or Inductor epilogue/prologue fusion within its template set.

expected_impact_on_megabake.item: RMSNorm into the following GEMM's prologue, with the sum of squares produced by the previous residual-add epilogue or by a cluster-DSMEM row reduction (the mega_mhc / all_reduce_mhc pattern)
expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: SmolLM-1.7B decode: 49 norms x 2.8 us = ~137 us of 2,983 us kernel time, plus ~1-2 barrier intervals per layer x 24 layers x 0.7 us = 17-34 us. Realistic saving 80-150 us (3-5%) after paying prologue cost inside 24 x 2 GEMMs. 135M (30 layers, 576-wide): norms are a larger share of 1,503 us, so 5-8% [uncertain].
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: The norm's FLOPs are trivial; its cost is a latency-bound phase plus a barrier. Moving the scale into the A-operand load (swapAB B-operand for tokens) costs one multiply per element loaded from SMEM.

expected_impact_on_megabake.item: Weight TMA/L2 prefetch issued before the activation dependency (fused_wo_a's pre-PDL TMA, ROADMAP step 9)
expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: 1.7B decode GEMMs run at ~1.8 TB/s vs ~2.2 TB/s slice peak. Closing half the gap on ~1.9 ms of GEMM time saves ~0.15-0.2 ms (5-7%). Pipeline fill per GEMM phase (~1-2 us x ~7 GEMM phases/layer x 24) bounds the same order [uncertain].
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: The first K stages of each GEMM phase start only after the barrier. Prefetching weights for phase i+1 during the barrier wait of phase i hides the fill.

expected_impact_on_megabake.item: Split-K reduced within a cluster through DSMEM (fused_wo_a's st.async peer reduction) instead of global FP32 partials
expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: Matters for narrow projections with fewer 64-row tiles than 60 SMs (135M: hidden 576 -> 9 tiles; k/v projections with few KV heads). Could turn the measured 'no gain' split-K into a 5-15% gain on those GEMMs, i.e. ~20-60 us on 135M decode [uncertain].
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: MegaBake's split-K writes FP32 partials and has the last split re-read them, adding HBM/L2 traffic and serialization. A DSMEM reduction keeps partials on-chip and needs no extra pass, but limits splits to the cluster size (<= 8 portable on SM90).

expected_impact_on_megabake.item: Lamport/data-sentinel polling for row-parallel producer->consumer chains (e.g. norm -> GEMM tile, attention -> o_proj tile) as a lighter form of event counters
expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: Each replaced grid barrier saves up to ~0.7 us. Replacing 2-3 of ~6 intervals per layer saves 1.4-2.1 us/layer: 135M ~40-60 us (3-4%), 1.7B ~35-50 us (1-2%) [uncertain].
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: Polling on data removes the counter and fence round trip, but only works when the consumer knows exactly which fragments it needs and the producer writes them with sentinel-free values (canonicalize -0.0).

expected_impact_on_megabake.item: Speculative decoding (multi-row verify on the existing <= 64-row swapAB path, optional in-kernel draft loop)
expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: Per-step kernel time for T = 4 vs T = 1 on weight-bound decode should rise only modestly (swapAB 16-row tile already covers T <= 16). At 60-70% acceptance with k = 3 that is ~2x tokens/s, the largest potential end-to-end gain, but it needs a draft model per target [uncertain].
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: MegaBake decode is weight-bandwidth bound (GEMMs ~65-80% of kernel time), so extra verify rows are nearly free.

expected_impact_on_megabake.item: Layout propagation / load-time weight permutation and RoPE folded into attention
expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: Removes 1 RoPE phase per layer (24 x ~2-3 us = 50-70 us on 1.7B) if RoPE is folded into the attention body's Q/K load [uncertain].
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: vLLM's own measurement shows such fusion helps only where the fused work is not dominated by padding. Measure under one launch, not eager.

expected_impact_on_megabake.estimate: No effect on the BF16 tested models. Needed only if FP8 checkpoints are targeted, in which case it halves activation traffic (minor at decode, where weights dominate).
expected_impact_on_megabake.reasoning: Decode bytes are dominated by weights. FP8 weights would matter far more than FP8 activations.

generality_and_overfitting_risk: vLLM side (cautionary examples of hand overfit): almost every fused op is gated on exact shapes or topology and falls back to a generic path when the gate fails. AllReduceMHC requires TP == 4, hidden_size == 5120, hc_mult == 4 and NVLink multicast (mhc.py:59-72), with a hard-coded cluster of 5 x 128 threads from FlashInfer's GB300 H5120 presets (all_reduce_mhc.py:882-945). MHC_OVERLAP_MAX_TOKENS = 16 was measured on GB200 TP4 (mhc.py:36). Mega mHC requires SM100, hidden % 1024 == 0 and hc == 4 (mega_mhc.py:17-28). Fused WO-A hard-codes head 512 = 448 NoPE + 64 RoPE (fused_wo_a.py:37-38, o_proj.py:38) and token limits 96/32 by CTA count (o_proj.py:18-26). Engram thresholds are 'Measured on GB200' with other GPUs disabled (engram.py:93-99), and the background grid uses num_SMs // 2 (engram.py:1140-1142). FlashMLA pads h_q to 64/128 (flashmla.py:71-78). The decoder-replay graph size ladder is a heuristic (decoder_replay_cudagraph.py:204-213). The lesson for a generic compiler: vLLM gets speed by writing one kernel per (model, topology, GPU) and guarding it. MegaBake should instead own the generic transforms these kernels instantiate: prologue/epilogue fusion, cluster split-K, layout propagation, off-critical-path scheduling, and data-flag sync. Their parameters should be chosen by search or a cost model per target, never by constants. MegaBake side, constants in this area that look tuned to SmolLM/Qwen2 on the 60-SM slice: SWAP_AB_MAX_ROWS = 64 and SWAP_AB_ROW_TILES = (16, 32, 64), justified by a 60-SM measurement comment (src/megabake/bodies/gemm.py:1888-1896). SPLIT_K_MAX = 16 and SPLIT_K_MIN_K_TILES = 2, with split-K disabled globally because it showed 'no gain on the 60-SM slice' (gemm.py:1899-1918; ROADMAP.md:173). It is plausibly a win on a full 132-SM H200 or with a DSMEM reduction, so a global off switch is an overfit decision. 'max_admitted_workers': 60 and resident-range timings recorded in the GEMM body provenance (gemm.py:2226-2238). This looks like measurement metadata rather than a hard limit, since TargetFacts.multiprocessor_count exists (bodies/interface.py:13-21) [uncertain]. small_m = rows <= 16 in planner (planner.py:453-455). Fold limits _FOLD_MAX_ROUNDS_PER_PHASE = 2, _FOLD_MAX_ROUNDS = 6, _FOLD_MAX_PHASES = 6 (schedule.py:1384-1386) were tuned on 135M's interval structure. The RMSNorm matcher keys on HF LlamaRMSNorm's cast order (regions.py:750). How to de-risk: (1) derive thresholds from TargetFacts (SM count, SMEM, cluster limits) plus a roofline cost model. (2) Autotune per bucket at compile time over a small candidate set (swapAB tile, split-K factor including DSMEM split-K, fold depth), as vLLM's warmup registry pre-compiles every dispatchable key (fused_wo_a.py:526-536) but with timing-based selection. (3) Keep a regression matrix that includes a non-MIG full GPU and at least one model with different hidden/head geometry (e.g. GQA with 1-2 KV heads, hidden not a multiple of 1024) before shipping any new constant.
hardware_portability: SM100-only in this catalogue: fused_wo_a (tcgen05.mma_mxfp8, tcgen05.cp, TMEM alloc/dealloc, cvt.rp.satfinite.ue8m0x2, 128B-swizzle SM100 descriptors with bit-46 version), DeepGEMM mega_mhc, FlashMLA mega attention and FP8 sparse decode paths. SM90-portable patterns: thread-block clusters with DSMEM (mapa.shared::cluster, st.shared::cluster, cluster_arrive_relaxed/cluster_wait; SM90 supports clusters up to 8 portable / 16 non-portable), st.async with mbarrier transaction counting, PDL (griddepcontrol on SM90+), TMA, multimem/NVLS (SM90 + NVSwitch). For MegaBake on SM90, cluster split-K and cluster row reductions map to WGMMA bodies with cluster_shape > 1, and FP8 block scaling would need software scale application (WGMMA has no MX block scaling). SM80-portable: the Lamport data-flag protocol (ld.volatile/st.global), vectorized raw loads/stores, prologue/epilogue fusion and layout permutation. There are no clusters on SM80, so cross-CTA reductions fall back to global atomics or barriers. SM100 lesson for MegaBake's blackwell.py: TMEM is a per-SM allocation that a co-resident kernel can hold. A persistent megakernel should allocate TMEM once at kernel start and keep it for the kernel's lifetime (relinquish_tmem_alloc_permit). Mixing PDL with TMEM allocation needs the ordering fused_wo_a uses (fused_wo_a.py:230-235). To stay target-generic: express each pattern as a capability-gated body variant (cluster size, DSMEM, block-scaled MMA, TMEM) selected from TargetFacts, with a non-cluster fallback, so the same IR lowers to SM80/SM90/SM100.
